blocks.text: In 1954 the psychologist Paul Fitts showed that the time needed to point at a target depends on two things: how far away it is and how big it is. More than seventy years later, the same relationship explains why some buttons feel effortless and others feel fiddly.
The version most often used in human-computer interaction is the Shannon formulation, popularised by Scott MacKenzie:

MT is the movement time, D is the distance to the centre of the target, W is the width of the target along the direction of movement, and a and b are constants measured for a particular device and user. The logarithmic term is called the **index of difficulty** and is measured in bits.

Moving 400 pixels to a button 20 pixels wide gives an index of difficulty of log2(400 / 20 + 1) = log2(21) ≈ 4.39 bits. Widening the button to 80 pixels reduces it to log2(6) ≈ 2.58 bits. The constants decide how many milliseconds that saves, but the direction never changes: the wider target is easier to hit.

items: Bigger targets are faster to hit, which matters most on touch screens.
Closer targets are faster to reach, so place related actions near where attention already is.
Screen edges behave like infinitely deep targets for a mouse, because the pointer stops at the edge. That is why menus along the very top of the screen are quick to reach.
Tightly packed small targets increase errors, not just time.

blocks.text: Fitts's law does not cover everything. It describes pointing, not reading, deciding, or remembering. But whenever an interface asks someone to move a pointer or a finger to a target, it is a reliable guide.
